Q28137011.summary: This small boxwood casket is carved on every side with scenes from the life of Christ. On the lid Christ hangs on the cross between angels, with mourners gathered below; on the side beneath, the Christ Child lies swaddled in the manger, flanked by standing figures. The other faces show the Ascension, Christ in Majesty, the Baptism and the Entry into Jerusalem, so that the little box carries the whole story of Christ's life, from crib to cross and glory.
facts: The Cleveland Museum calls the casket a rare, if not unique, example of high-quality woodcarving from Anglo-Saxon England; it may have held relics.

Its lid was found at Uttoxeter, Staffordshire, in the early 19th century, and its base was bought in Cheshire in 1921; the reunited casket was lent to the Victoria and Albert Museum from 1937 to 1953.
In the Ascension scene, the museum notes, God's hand is shown pulling Christ heavenward.

cur:catacombs-sarcophagus-31551.summary: Around a shell with the portraits of a couple, two registers present miracles of Christ, scenes of Peter and Old Testament types of salvation in tight succession. Parts of the relief are restorations, but the composition preserves the full Constantinian programme of Christian hope.
facts: According to Commons, it was found in 1592 in the Vigna Guidaschi near San Sebastiano on the Via Appia.
Commons notes that the front is partly restored.
cur:catacombs-sarcophagus-31551.notes: Commons gives the date variously as '330–25' (file name) and 300–330 (description).

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Two figures sit side by side on green globes within blue medallions: at the left the Lord, now badly flaked, and at the right the haloed, bearded Christ in a golden mantle, who raises his hand in speech. The image illustrates the psalm Christ himself quoted of the Messiah: 'The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand'.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature. The left figure has largely lost its paint.

Q473843.summary: The jewelled front of this processional cross bears an ancient cameo of Augustus, but its plain gold reverse is engraved with the crucified Christ, his head sunk upon his shoulder and his body sagging in death. Above him the hand of God holds a wreath enclosing the dove of the Holy Spirit, and medallions at the ends of the arms hold the mourning sun and moon. The contrast is deliberate: imperial splendour on one side, the suffering Saviour on the other.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the hand of God with a wreath enclosing the dove is the earliest known appearance of this motif, which brings the whole Trinity into the Crucifixion.
The cross takes its name from a rock-crystal seal of the Carolingian king Lothair II set near its base, though it was made over a century after his death, possibly for Otto III.
It is still carried in procession on high feast days and placed beside the main altar of Aachen Cathedral.
Q473843.notes: Only the engraved side depicts Christ; Wikipedia notes that some sources call this the front, since the cross may have been carried with the Crucifixion facing forward.

cur:objects2-walters-oil-flask-megale.summary: This tall silver flask is decorated in relief with standing figures of Christ, the Virgin and two military saints, perhaps Sergios and Bacchos, rendered with the soft, voluminous drapery and large eyes of Byzantine Syria. Its inscription records that Megale and her family gave it in fulfilment of a vow and for the repose of the souls of Heliodorus and Acacius. It probably held consecrated oil for baptism or for anointing the sick and dying.
facts: The Greek inscription reads, in translation: 'For the prayer and salvation of Megale and of her children and nephews, and for the repose of the soul of Heliodorus and Acacius.'
According to the Walters provenance, it was excavated in Syria in 1908–1910 and reached Henry Walters in 1929.
cur:objects2-walters-oil-flask-megale.notes: The photograph shows the side with the Virgin; Christ is on another side of the flask, as described by the museum.
